edits.before: description: "THE single visual acceptance pass for a rendered deliverable of these types only — pptx, docx, xlsx, pdf, poster, chart; for anything else, do not use it. Use it *instead of* looking at the page images yourself, never in addition: pick one gate — spawn visual-judge, or (only if visual-judge is unavailable) inspect the images yourself — and do not pre-screen the pages before dispatching, because a preliminary look followed by a visual-judge call duplicates the same review and wastes a full render pass. Its bar is user acceptance: it judges everything the user will see on its assigned pages — visual asset quality and layout & composition — and returns one JSON verdict line per page (pass/fail + evidence-backed issues; a clean programmatic/script check is no cover and no substitute). It is read-only and edits nothing; it can only Read pre-rendered page PNGs (never pptx/docx/HTML/PDF opened as images), so render the pages to PNG, hand visual-judge the paths, and act on its verdicts — those verdicts are the visual gate's result, not an input to your own re-judging. Dispatch grouping, what to pass in, and the repair loop follow the delivery protocol's visual gate in your system prompt."
edits.after: description: "THE single visual acceptance pass for a rendered deliverable of these types only — pptx, docx, xlsx, pdf, poster, chart; for anything else, do not use it. Use it *instead of* looking at the page images yourself, never in addition: pick one gate — spawn visual-judge, or (only if visual-judge is unavailable) inspect the images yourself — and do not pre-screen the pages before dispatching, because a preliminary look followed by a visual-judge call duplicates the same review and wastes a full render pass. Its bar is user acceptance: it judges everything the user will see on its assigned pages — visual asset quality and layout & composition — and returns one JSON verdict line per page (pass/fail + evidence-backed issues; a clean programmatic/script check is no cover and no substitute). It is read-only and edits nothing; it can only inspect pre-rendered page PNGs via view_workspace_file (never pptx/docx/HTML/PDF opened as images), so render the pages to PNG, hand visual-judge the paths, and act on its verdicts — those verdicts are the visual gate's result, not an input to your own re-judging. Dispatch grouping, what to pass in, and the repair loop follow the AILab visual gate (planned:P2; the source delivery protocol is not supplied)."

1. `open_document(path, at?)` opens the file in the panel and returns its outline. Open the document before discussing it so the user sees what you see.
2. `read_document(anchor, cursor?)` returns the paragraphs and tables (as markdown) of a location. Read the relevant part before answering; follow the `cursor` hint for long content instead of guessing.
3. `search_document(path, query)` finds text and returns paragraph and table anchors.
4. `show_in_viewer(targets, note?)` scrolls the panel to the targets and highlights them. Use it whenever your answer is about specific places, e.g. after finding the clauses you discuss. Add `quote` (exact text inside the paragraph) to highlight a phrase in a long paragraph. Keep `note` to one short sentence.
5. `get_view()` tells you what the user is looking at and what they selected. Call it when the user says "this", "here", "the selected …" or similar without an anchor.
6. `capture_view(anchor?)` (a panel tool, available while the panel is open) returns an image of the rendered location. Use it when layout, images or formatting matter. The document must already be open in the panel.

4. `planned:P3 show_in_viewer(targets, note?)` scrolls the panel to the targets and highlights them. Use it whenever your answer is about specific places, e.g. after finding the clauses you discuss. Add `quote` (exact text inside the paragraph) to highlight a phrase in a long paragraph. Keep `note` to one short sentence.
5. `planned:P3 get_view()` tells you what the user is looking at and what they selected. Call it when the user says "this", "here", "the selected …" or similar without an anchor.

edits.before: description: "THE single visual acceptance pass for a rendered deliverable of these types only — pptx, docx, xlsx, pdf, poster, chart; for anything else, do not use it. Use it *instead of* looking at the page images yourself, never in addition: pick one gate — spawn visual-judge, or (only if visual-judge is unavailable) inspect the images yourself — and do not pre-screen the pages before dispatching, because a preliminary look followed by a visual-judge call duplicates the same review and wastes a full render pass. Its bar is user acceptance: it judges everything the user will see on its assigned pages — visual asset quality and layout & composition — and returns one JSON verdict line per page (pass/fail + evidence-backed issues; a clean programmatic/script check is no cover and no substitute). It is read-only and edits nothing; it can only Read pre-rendered page PNGs (never pptx/docx/HTML/PDF opened as images), so render the pages to PNG, hand visual-judge the paths, and act on its verdicts — those verdicts are the visual gate's result, not an input to your own re-judging. Dispatch grouping, what to pass in, and the repair loop follow the delivery protocol's visual gate in your system prompt."
edits.after: description: "THE single visual acceptance pass for a rendered deliverable of these types only — pptx, docx, xlsx, pdf, poster, chart; for anything else, do not use it. Use it *instead of* looking at the page images yourself, never in addition: pick one gate — spawn visual-judge, or (only if visual-judge is unavailable) inspect the images yourself — and do not pre-screen the pages before dispatching, because a preliminary look followed by a visual-judge call duplicates the same review and wastes a full render pass. Its bar is user acceptance: it judges everything the user will see on its assigned pages — visual asset quality and layout & composition — and returns one JSON verdict line per page (pass/fail + evidence-backed issues; a clean programmatic/script check is no cover and no substitute). It is read-only and edits nothing; it can only inspect pre-rendered page PNGs via view_workspace_file (never pptx/docx/HTML/PDF opened as images), so render the pages to PNG, hand visual-judge the paths, and act on its verdicts — those verdicts are the visual gate's result, not an input to your own re-judging. Dispatch grouping, what to pass in, and the repair loop follow the AILab visual gate (planned:P2; the source delivery protocol is not supplied)."

edits.before:
1. `open_document(path, at?)` opens the deck in the panel and returns its outline. Open it before discussing it so the user sees what you see.
2. `read_document(anchor, cursor?)` returns the slides of a location with their shapes' text and speaker notes. Read the relevant slides before answering; follow the `cursor` hint for long decks instead of guessing.
3. `search_document(path, query)` finds text and returns shape anchors.
4. `show_in_viewer(targets, note?)` scrolls the panel to the targets and highlights them. Use it whenever your answer is about specific slides or shapes, e.g. when you point out inconsistent numbers. Keep `note` to one short sentence.
5. `get_view()` tells you which slide the user is looking at and what they selected. Call it when the user says "this", "here", "this slide" or similar without an anchor.
6. `capture_view(anchor?)` (a panel tool, available while the panel is open) returns an image of the rendered slide. Use it when layout, images, charts or visual design matter, which on slides is often. The deck must already be open in the panel.

5. `planned:P3 get_view()` tells you which slide the user is looking at and what they selected. Call it when the user says "this", "here", "this slide" or similar without an anchor.
